ad6_redlining.topic: HOLC, FHA underwriting, GI Bill, Levittown covenants, the 30-year mortgage, fair-housing law, zoning

claims.text: Before the Great Depression US home mortgages typically ran 5-10 years, were not amortised (principal due in a lump sum), carried mostly variable rates and loan-to-value of 50% or less; borrowers typically renegotiated every year
About 250,000 foreclosures a year 1931-1935; at the worst nearly 10% of homes were in foreclosure

HOLC bought defaulted mortgages and converted about one million into fixed-rate, 20-year, fully amortising loans; FHA initially insured loans up to 20 years and 80% LTV; in 1948 the maximum term rose to 30 years; in 1956 maximum LTV rose to 95% (new) and 90% (existing)
Homeownership rose from 43.6% in 1940 to 64% by 1980

FHA Underwriting Manual (1938) s.980(3) listed among recommended restrictions 'prohibition of the occupancy of properties except by the race for which they are intended'; s.982(1) said schools 'should not be attended in large numbers by inharmonious racial groups'
HOLC graded neighbourhoods A-D on 'residential security' maps made 1935-1940

Fishback, Rose, Snowden and Storrs: HOLC had made 90% of its loans before its map project began in 1935; 'very unlikely' the HOLC maps guided lending; FHA red lines 'likely far more impactful', FHA redlined core urban neighbourhoods 'from day one'; in Baltimore 1935-1940 FHA insured loans for only about 25 Black households

Aaronson, Hartley and Mazumder: lower HOLC grades associated with lower later homeownership, house values and rents and higher Black share; gaps rose until about 1970-1980 then declined; D-C boundary homeownership gap fell after 1990
Katznelson: GI Bill benefits administered locally; of 3,229 GI Bill guaranteed home, business and farm loans made in Mississippi in 1947, two went to Black veterans (Ebony survey of 13 cities)
Turner and Bound: GI Bill raised college attainment of Black men born outside the South by about 0.4 years; few gains for Southern-born Black men; it widened the Southern Black-white gap
Levittown lease clause barred occupancy by 'any person other than members of the Caucasian race'; first Levittown built from 1947
Levittown houses sold from about $8,000; up-front cost about $400 for many with GI Bill/federal backing; by 1951 17,447 Levitt homes in the area; clause 25 of the lease

Shelley v. Kraemer (1948): courts cannot enforce racially restrictive covenants; National Housing Act 1934 created FHA; Housing Act 1949 goal 'a decent home and a suitable living environment for every American family'; Fair Housing Act enacted 11 April 1968; Jones v. Mayer 1968; Fair Housing Amendments Act 1988

Nonfarm homeownership rose from 41% (1940) to 61% (1960), about 60% of the rise before 1947; VA loans from 1944 raised aggregate homeownership about 7% (Fetter); white homeownership in the bottom income tercile was flat 1947-1960; FHA down payments at least 20% 1947-1954, cut to 5-16% by the Housing Act of 1954
Homeownership 1960: white 65%, Black 38% (gap 27 points); 2022: 74.6% vs 45.3% (gap about 29)
Glaeser and Gyourko (2018): where prices sit well above construction cost the gap acts as a 'regulatory tax' that in many areas appears to exceed any reasonable externality cost of new construction

FEDS Note Table 2: FHA mortgages held by 13.4% of all owners in the bottom income tercile vs 20.5% in the top tercile (recent buyers 12.9% vs 22.4%); VA mortgages raised the aggregate homeownership rate 'by about 7 percent' (Fetter 2013).
Turner and Bound: WWII service plus GI benefits raised white men's attainment about 0.3 years of college; Black men born outside the South about 0.4 years; few gains for Southern-born Black men.
Euclid v. Ambler (decided 22 Nov 1926, Sutherland J.): upheld a zoning ordinance excluding apartment houses from residential districts; 'very often the apartment house is a mere parasite'.

NYT Upshot (Badger and Bui, 18 June 2019): it is illegal on 75 percent of the residential land in many American cities to build anything other than a detached single-family home (UrbanFootprint data).

Reason (Mar 2023): Minneapolis first jurisdiction to eliminate single-family-only zoning, late 2018 (in force 2020), 104 new duplex/triplex units in first two years; Oregon, California and Maine passed statewide laws allowing at least duplexes on almost all residential land; California SB 9 effective Jan 2022, Terner Center found construction limited or non-existent in 13 cities (LA 38 approvals, SF 4); Portland 127 units Aug 2021–Feb 2022.
Oregon Legislature passed HB 2001 (June/July 2019), requiring cities to allow duplexes and in larger cities other middle housing in single-family zones.

Washington HB 1110 signed 8 May 2023: cities of 25,000–75,000 must allow duplexes in all residential zones (fourplexes near transit or with affordability); over 75,000 fourplexes everywhere, sixplexes near transit or with two affordable units.
Levittown NY: Levitt began spring 1947 and by November 1951 had built 17,447 houses; homes sold for under $8,000 with 5% down, 0% for veterans; clause 25 barred occupancy by non-Caucasians.
Levittown NY census: 57 Black residents of 65,276 in 1960 (Lizabeth Cohen); 45 of 57,045 in 1980; 387 of 53,067 in 2000.

ad6_price.topic: Price-to-income, homeownership series, first-time buyers, rent burden, mortgage rates, institutional investors

claims.text: JCHS (2013 method, NAR 1991 prices indexed by FHFA): long-run average price-to-income 3.65; 2006 peak 4.63; 2011 low 3.26
JCHS (2018): typical existing single-family price to median household income 3.2 in 1988; 3.1-3.4 across 1980-1999; 4.7 in 2005, the highest since at least 1980; 3.3 in 2011; 4.2 in 2017
JCHS (January 2024): national ratio 5.6 in 2022, a record since the early 1970s; 4.1 in 2019

NAR 2025 Profile: first-time buyers 21% of purchases (record low), median age 40 (record high); repeat buyers median age 62; survey of 173,250 recent buyers mailed July 2025, 6,103 responses, adjusted response rate 3.5%, covering July 2024-June 2025; share has fallen about 50% since 2007

JCHS 2026 (released 17 June 2026): 22.7m renter households (49%) cost-burdened (>30% of income) in 2024, a record; units under $1,000 fell 30% from 8.3m (2014) to 5.8m (2024); rents fell 0.5% y/y in Q1 2026 but professionally managed asking rents 29% above 2020; rents fell in most Southern and Western markets; build-to-rent 11% of new single-family homes in 2025; home insurance premiums +72% 2019-2025
30-year fixed mortgage average 7.40% on 15 October 2026, vs 6.27% a year earlier (Freddie Mac PMMS)

GAO 2024: no investor owned 1,000+ single-family rentals in late 2011; 170,000-300,000 homes by 2015; studies suggest institutional investors may have contributed to rising prices and rents and helped stabilise neighbourhoods after the crisis; no consistent definition
GAO via NLIHC: by 2022, 32 institutional investors owned about 450,000 homes (five largest nearly 300,000), about 2% of US single-family rental stock nationally and about 25% in the Atlanta metro

CRS 2026: institutional investors own roughly 3-5% of single-family rental homes nationally (1,000+ homes about 3% per GAO/Urban 2022; 350+ about 5% per John Burns 2026); Census RHFS 2024: of 15.7m one-unit rentals about three-quarters owned by entities with 10 or fewer, under 2% by entities with over 100; investors of all sizes about 30% of SF purchases Dec 2025 (Cotality), large and mega about 3% each; Redfin 19% Q1 2026; GAO-26-108675 found market fundamentals drove rent increases in six metros; larger landlords file more evictions

Executive Order 14376 'Stopping Wall Street from Competing with Main Street Homebuyers', 20 January 2026: directed agencies to stop facilitating large-investor purchases and Treasury to define terms; not an outright ban

21st Century ROAD to Housing Act (H.R. 6644) signed 11 July 2026: bars entities controlling 350+ single-family homes from buying more, with exemptions (build-to-rent, new or renovated homes, foreclosures, 55+ communities); penalty greater of $1m or 3x purchase price; takes effect 180 days after enactment; repealed after 15 years

JCHS (October 2025): national median single-family price to median household income 3.2 throughout the 1990s, 4.1 in 2019, 5.0 in 2024; prices +48% vs incomes +22% 2019-2024; text says 'nearly matching previous record highs' while the figure caption says 'back to a record'
Audit re-fetch (22 Oct 2026) of FRED RHORUSQ156N first-quarter values used in the series file: 1965 62.9; 1975 64.4; 2004 Q1 68.6 (Q2 69.2); 2016 Q1 63.5 (Q2 62.9); 2026 Q1 65.3, Q2 65.0.
Book arithmetic (standard amortisation, 360 payments, per $100,000): 3.00% $421.6; 6.27% $617.0; 7.40% $692.4 a month; 692.4/421.6 = 1.64.

ad6_eviction.topic: Eviction prevalence, record accuracy, tenant screening, contract-for-deed, RealPage, homelessness

claims.text: Gromis et al. (PNAS 2022): about 3.6m eviction cases filed a year on average 2000-2018, about 2.7m households (repeat filings); households threatened peaked about 7.5% 2005-2008, about 6% recently

Eviction Lab tracking system (48 sites, about one-third of renter households, not nationally representative): 1.23m filings in 2025 vs 1.26m in 2024, 3.2% below the post-pandemic (2023-24) average; average filing rate 8.0%, about one in 13 renter households; Travis County TX +27%
Porton, Gromis and Desmond (2021): about 22% of eviction records on average in 3.6m records from 12 states contain ambiguous outcome information or misstate the tenant's history

CFPB Nov 2022: 'no definitive analysis of the frequency of matching errors'; describes wildcard matching on partial names, over-inclusion, sealed records, one case appearing as two; court-record pulls rarely cost over $1 vs about $7 for manual checks; only 5 of 17 firms advertised manual verification; cites Porton et al. for 22% 'ambiguous or false' and Gromis et al. for 3.6m records; serial filings over 20% of cases in at least four states; corporate landlords file at 'substantially higher' rates (Fed study); about $1.3bn industry revenue estimate

FTC/CFPB v. TransUnion Rental Screening Solutions (12 Oct 2023): alleged reporting one eviction case as several, omitting dismissals, labelling landlord claims 'Judgment Amount', including sealed records; $15m total ($11m redress, $4m penalty), largest FTC tenant-screening recovery

Evicted (Desmond, Crown, March 2016; Milwaukee fieldwork 2008-09, eight families) won the 2017 Pulitzer Prize in General Nonfiction; board: evictions 'less a consequence than a cause of poverty'; critics (e.g. Christian Schneider, Milwaukee Journal Sentinel) argued eviction exacerbates existing problems rather than causing poverty
Shelterforce 2018 critique (Aiello et al.): Eviction Lab undercounts evictions by not working with housing-justice groups

Duke Cook Center (2019): 75-95% of homes sold to Black families in Chicago in the 1950s-60s sold on contract; 84% markup over sellers' purchase price; $587/month (2019 $) more than a fair FHA/conventional loan; average real markup $71,727 per home; total $3.2-4.0bn (2019 $; also given as $3.1-3.9bn); buyer accrues no equity, missed payment can mean eviction and forfeiture

Pew (2022 survey): about 36m Americans have used alternative home financing (land contracts etc.), about 7m at the time; deals usually unrecorded, not regulated like mortgages; Pennsylvania AG case: 285 homes ordered deeded to Vision Property Management customers

Harbour Portfolio bought foreclosed homes in bulk mostly from Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac and resold them on contracts for deed 2012-2016 to buyers unable to get conventional financing; CFPB June 2020 penalties $25,000 (Harbour) and $10,000 (NAA/NAM) for credit-reporting deception; Atlanta resales $40,000-50,000 at about 10% over 30 years; sales concentrated in tracts 86.25% African American; Atlanta Legal Aid suit settled

DOJ and 8 states (NC, CA, CO, CT, MN, OR, TN, WA) sued RealPage 23 Aug 2024 in M.D.N.C. under Sherman Act ss.1-2, alleging landlords share nonpublic rent data, auto-accept and advisors enforce adherence; alleged about 80% share of commercial revenue-management software for multifamily

Proposed DOJ-RealPage settlement 24 Nov 2025: no competitors' nonpublic data in real-time pricing; training only on nonpublic data at least 12 months old; no models narrower than state level; remove features limiting rent decreases; court-appointed monitor; cooperation
NC federal judge approved DOJ-RealPage final judgment (reported 20 May 2026); no admission of wrongdoing; North Carolina's state case still active
Class action (M.D. Tenn., Judge Waverly Crenshaw): final approval of $359,925,000 settlements with 41 landlord defendants, reported 16 Oct 2026

New York S.7882 (signed Oct 2025, effective Dec 2025) bans algorithmic rent-setting coordination; SDNY granted RealPage a preliminary injunction on First Amendment grounds (late Sept 2026); case continues

HUD Jan 2025 PIT: 745,652 homeless (479,332 sheltered, 266,320 unsheltered), down from 771,480 in 2024; chronically homeless individuals 155,750 a record; veterans 32,495 lowest since 2009; 2016 low 549,928; one-night snapshot; 29 of almost 400 CoCs did no unsheltered count in 2025

Atlanta Legal Aid: Harbour bought hundreds of homes in Atlanta and thousands nationwide, mostly from Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, sometimes for as little as $10,000; complaint filed for seventeen African-American consumers; settlement gave actual damages and restructured mortgages.

Humphries et al. (Cook County court records linked to credit data, judge-leniency design): financial strain is high and rises sharply before a filing for evicted and non-evicted tenants alike; eviction reduces credit access and durable consumption for several years, but the effects are small relative to that prior strain.
Evicted 'takes us into the poorest neighborhoods of Milwaukee to tell the story of eight families on the edge'.
